slot.brief: Rank or pick the odd one out among given amines in aqueous basicity (aliphatic vs aniline vs ammonia type comparison); purely conceptual, no pKa values.

stem: Considering the electronic effects of the phenyl ring, which of the following compounds is the strongest base in an aqueous medium?

verdicts.working: In aniline, N-methylaniline and diphenylamine the N lone pair is delocalized into the ring(s), reducing basicity (diphenylamine worst, two rings). In benzylamine the CH2 spacer prevents conjugation, so the lone pair is fully available; pKa of conjugate acids: benzylammonium ≈ 9.3 vs anilinium ≈ 4.6, N-methylanilinium ≈ 4.85, diphenylammonium ≈ 0.8. Benzylamine is the strongest base in water.

working:
In benzylamine ($	ext{C}_6	ext{H}_5	ext{CH}_2	ext{NH}_2$), the amino group ($-	ext{NH}_2$) is attached to an $sp^3$-hybridised carbon ($-	ext{CH}_2-$). Because of this intervening methylene group, the lone pair on the nitrogen atom cannot enter into resonance with the $\pi$-system of the benzene ring. Benzylamine therefore acts as an aliphatic amine, retaining a localised lone pair available for protonation ($pK_b \approx 4.70$).

In contrast, in aniline ($	ext{C}_6	ext{H}_5	ext{NH}_2$), $N$-methylaniline ($	ext{C}_6	ext{H}_5	ext{NHCH}_3$), and diphenylamine ($(	ext{C}_6	ext{H}_5)_2	ext{NH}$), the nitrogen atom is bonded directly to the $sp^2$-hybridised aromatic ring. The lone pair is delocalised into the ring by resonance, drastically decreasing basicity ($pK_b > 9$ for all three).

Hence, benzylamine is by far the strongest base among the given choices.

Option A (Aniline): The nitrogen lone pair is delocalised over the benzene ring via resonance, making it much less basic than an aliphatic amine.
